entries.title: 4 wounded in Auburn Gresham shooting
entries.summary: <p>Four people were wounded in a shooting Saturday evening in Auburn Gresham, Chicago police said.</p><p>The victims were on the sidewalk along the 8500 block of South Sangamon Street about 7:17 p.m. when a car pulled alongside them and multiple people in the vehicle fired several shots, police said.</p><p>A 43-year-old man suffered a gunshot wound to his left leg and was taken to University of Chicago Hospital in critical condition, police said.</p><p>A man whose age was unknown was shot in the abdomen and taken to Christ Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>A 34-year-old man was shot in the right leg and a 32-year-old woman suffered a graze wound to her left arm. They both declined treatment at the scene. </p><p>No arrests have been made. </p>

entries.title: Israel Abrams plans to lead No. 4 Montini to a championship three-peat
entries.summary: <p>Montini senior Israel Abrams is one of the best quarterbacks in the country, ranked among the top four by all the national recruiting services. He is also a top-tier talker, quick to turn a phrase that cries out for a headline:</p><p>‘‘We have one mentality, and that is to kill.’’</p><p>‘‘We are going to go 38-0, we will win three state titles and stamp our name in history.’’</p><p>‘‘I don’t have to worry about the guys on this team. The coaches stay locked in, and so do the guys. It is a well-oiled machine.’’</p><p>It is worth noting all the ‘‘wes’’ in those bold statements and all the team goals mentioned. Abrams, a Miami recruit, isn’t thinking about raising his profile a notch to be named the top quarterback in the country. He isn’t boasting about his five-star ranking. He is focused on winning.</p><p>‘‘He’s a coach’s dream,’’ Montini coach Mike Bukovsky said. ‘‘He loves to play the game. We’ve never had one instance or issue with him not wanting to practice or anything like that. He always loves to compete, to challenge himself and to be challenged.’’</p><p>Abrams is 6-4 and nearing 200 pounds. Bukovsky is thrilled with the weight and muscle Abrams added during the offseason after he threw for 4,072 yards and led the Broncos to an undefeated season and the Class 4A state title in 2025. Abrams was 233-for-340 with 40 touchdown passes and six interceptions. entries.title: Matt Shaw expected to head out on rehab assignment this week
entries.summary: <p>Matt Shaw, slotted as the Cubs super-utility man this season, may be nearing a return from a sprained left hand that’s sidelined him since June 28.</p><p> </p><p>“I think we’re basically at a point where we’re considering a rehab assignment very soon, manager Craig Counsell said before Saturday’s 8-4 loss to St. Louis.</p><p> </p><p>At Triple-A Iowa maybe this week?</p><p> </p><p>“That’s what we’re on pace for,” Counsell said.</p><p> </p><p>Counsell said Shaw hit off a Trajekt high-velocity pitching machine and swung and missed, which is part of the rehab process. The manager said Shaw felt great on Friday and was scheduled to repeat the exercise on Saturday.</p><p> </p><p>Shaw was projected in the super-utility role after the Cubs signed third baseman Alex Bregman to his $175 million, five year free agent contract. Shaw has played six positions this season, with 26 game appearances in right field, followed by second base (seven games), third base (five games), left field (two games), first base (two games) and center field (one game).</p><p> </p><p>He stepped in as the Cubs primary right fielder for 12 games after Seiya Suzuki hurt his right knee on June 13.</p><p> </p><p>In 56 games, the 24-year-old Shaw is batting .246 with four homers and 20 RBIs. He's on his second stint on the IL, after sitting out May 20 to June 9 with mid-back tightness. </p><p> </p><p><b>Wrangling Over “The W”</b></p><p> </p><p>Major League Baseball doesn’t want the WNBA to have unchecked control of “The W.”</p><p> </p><p>The WNBA, its teams and players have been using “The W” to refer to the league in an overall branding strategy. In March 2025, the WNBA <a class="Link" href="https://tmsearch.uspto.gov/search/search-results/99105898" target="_blank" >filed a trademark application</a> for use of “The W” on apparel such as jersey, shirts and caps.</p><p> </p><p>With the Cubs and Washington Nationals in mind, Major League Baseball filed a joint opposition to the trademark application on Aug. 10 to slow the process down establish clear distinctions with versions of the “W” used by those two clubs.</p><p> </p><p>The concern: The WNBA’s use of the“The W” could create confusion and issues with the Cubs white-and-blue “W” win flags that fly on Wrigley Field’s center field scoreboard after victories. The Cubs use that “W” mark on a variety of merchandise. Even bigger, MLB wants to protect the Nationals’ primary script “W” logo that appears on the club’s caps and uniforms, as well as merchandise. </p><p> </p><p>MLB manages trademarks and intellectual property not only for itself and the National and American Leagues, but member teams through “consultation and conversation” with them.</p><p> </p><p>Published reports that originated with Front Office Sports, said MLB has been in regular contact with the WNBA and and NBA, which own 42 % of the women’s league. The goal is to establish boundaries for use of “The W” trademark.</p><p> </p><p>A source at MLB confirmed the businesslike and ongoing dialog, and that it has been amicable. MLB filed the joint opposition for more time to “hash out the details."</p><p> </p><p> </p><p><b>Palencia Progressing</b></p><p>Closer Daniel Palencia, out with right elbow inflammation since June 16, is making progress in his rehab process.</p><p></p><p>The right-hander is scheduled to pitch in Sunday for Triple-A Iowa after being elevated from Double-A Knoxville, where he tossed a strong scoreless inning on Thursday.</p><p></p><p>“He had a nice outing in Knoxville in his last one, and hopefully build on that again tomorrow in Iowa,” Counsell said.</p><p> </p><p><b>More Báez Banter</b></p><p>More on St. Louis outfielder Joshua Báez, who made history with homers in his first three major-league at-bats in Saturday’s 8-4 Cardinals win.</p><p>• Baez became the fourth player this season to go deep in his first major-league at bat, joining Cleveland’s Chase DeLauter, Philadelphia’s Felix Reyes and Detroit’s Eduardo Valencia.</p><p>• He became the sixth Cardinal to homer on the first pitch he ever faced. The most recent previously was pitcher Adam Wainwright, in 2006.<br></p>

entries.title: 4 wounded in Auburn Gresham shooting
entries.summary: <p>Four people were wounded in a shooting Saturday evening in Auburn Gresham, Chicago police said.</p><p>The victims were on the sidewalk along the 8500 block of South Sangamon Street about 7:17 p.m. when a car pulled alongside them and multiple people in the vehicle fired several shots, police said.</p><p>A 43-year-old man suffered a gunshot wound to his left leg and was taken to University of Chicago Hospital in critical condition, police said.</p><p>A man whose age was unknown was shot in the abdomen and taken to Christ Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>A 34-year-old man was shot in the right leg and a 32-year-old woman suffered a graze wound to her left arm. They both declined treatment at the scene. </p><p>No arrests have been made. </p>

entries.title: Blackhawks prospect rankings: Vaclav Nestrasil climbs to top spot after many graduations
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' pool of talented young players has not shrunk, but their prospect pool nevertheless has.</p><p>That's because so many of those young players graduated from prospects into NHL players during the past year. The Hawks' roster will be extremely young in 2026-27.</p><p>There will be at least seven forwards age 22 or younger — Connor Bedard, Frank Nazar, Anton Frondell, Roman Kantserov, Nick Lardis, Oliver Moore and Ryan Greene — and all project to occupy <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/26/projecting-blackhawks-lines-patrick-kane-bowen-byram-connor-bedard-frank-nazar" target="_blank" >top-nine roles</a>.</p><p>And among all of the defensemen and goalies, Ian Cole is the lone player older than 25. Prominent offseason addition Bowen Byram, 25, is actually eight days younger than Alex Vlasic. Artyom Levshunov, Sam Rinzel, Wyatt Kaiser and Arvid Soderblom are all younger than them, some considerably so, whereas Spencer Knight is two months older.</p><p>The majority of the Hawks' resources this season will go toward helping those young players learn, mature and hopefully eventually succeed in the NHL.</p><p>But prospect development remains important, too. The Hawks still have some holes to fill in their young core, and they need to keep a steady stream of prospects moving toward the NHL who can, over time, either replace departing veterans or offer value as trade chips.</p><p>Of the 20 Hawks prospects discussed in the Sun-Times' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/07/06/blackhawks-prospect-rankings-2025-sam-rinzel-artyom-levshunov-anton-frondell" target="_blank" >summer 2025 rankings</a>, six have since graduated into the NHL, three have been traded (Colton Dach, Nolan Allan and Jack Pridham) and two are in murky situations (Kevin Korchinski and Ethan Del Mastro). </p><p>That represents more than half the list, which means these new summer 2026 prospect rankings look a lot different — and overall less impressive. </p><p>But they're still substantial compared to many NHL teams, as well as to the Stan Bowman-era Hawks. Notably, the top six prospects below could all conceivably play NHL games sometime this season.</p><h3><b>1. Vaclav Nestrasil, forward, age 19</b></h3><p>Nestrasil, the 25th pick in 2025, has rapidly risen to the top of the pool. He blew away his own expectations for his freshman season at UMass, as his 31 points in 34 games ranked fifth among NCAA players 19 or younger.</p><p>The 6-6 winger is dangerous both on the rush and on the forecheck, and he's learning how to take advantage of his size. Hawks brass <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/05/blackhawks-prospects-vaclav-nestrasil-sacha-boisvert-mason-west-adam-gajan" target="_blank" >raved about him</a> this summer and will likely try to sign him after UMass' upcoming season.</p><h3><b>2. Sacha Boisvert, forward, 20</b></h3><p>Although Boisvert's 2025-26 season was disappointing, he flashed his potential as a North Dakota freshman in 2024-25, and he almost looks like a different person after bulking up his 6-3 frame this summer (from 190 pounds to 205). He will start this season in the AHL as one of Rockford's top forwards.</p><h3><b>3. John Mustard, forward, 20</b></h3><p>Mustard <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/03/10/blackhawks-prospects-john-mustard-julius-sumpf-providence-hockey" target="_blank" >improved</a> his shooting and decision-making as a Providence sophomore last season and translated that into production, recording 29 points in 36 games. He stood out at development camp this summer, too. The Hawks will try to sign the speedster after his upcoming junior year.</p><h3><b>4. Marek Vanacker, forward, 20</b></h3><p>Vanacker is angling to be the Hawks' next Tyler Bertuzzi as a high-efficiency <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/01/13/blackhawks-prospects-marek-vanacker-brantford-ohl-goals-mindset" target="_blank" >scorer</a> who excels in dirty areas around the net. He led the OHL in goals last season with 47 in 60 games (albeit as an overager), and he will attempt to translate that skill into the AHL this season.</p><h3><b>5. A.J. Spellacy, forward, 20</b></h3><p>The Hawks added NHL veterans Cole Smith and Jordan Greenway this summer to inject grit into their forward corps, but looking longer-term, Spellacy should help with that. The 6-3 winger is aggressive, physical and understands the value of penalty-killing. His role this season will be telling.</p><h3><b>12. Gavin Hayes, forward, 22</b></h3><p>Hayes and Savoie both tallied 26 points in roughly 60 games for Rockford last season. Hayes' production was steadily increasing, though, before an MCL injury in March cut his season short. His biggest strength is his hockey IQ.</p><h3><b>13. Martin Misiak, forward, 21</b></h3><p>Misiak is the only second-round pick among this foursome, but he initially struggled to crack Rockford's lineup last fall. He finished with 15 points in 63 games, and Rockford coach Jared Nightingale called him one of the team's most-improved players. He needs to continue that momentum.</p><h3><b>14. Adam Gajan, goalie, 22</b></h3><p></p><p>Gajan bounced back from a poor freshman season at Minnesota-Duluth in 2024-25 with a better sophomore season. He said he played deeper in the net, kept his shoulders more upright and trusted his size and technique more. He has turned pro and will compete with incumbent Stan Berezhnoy for Rockford's backup goalie job behind Commesso.</p><p></p><h3><b>15. Nathan Behm, forward, 19</b></h3><p>Behm is coming off a solid but unremarkable third WHL season. He will be a freshman this season at Arizona State, where his performance will be more indicative of his potential.</p><h3><b>16. Taige Harding, defenseman, 24</b></h3><p>Nightingale was impressed by the 6-foot-7 Harding's efforts to improve his skating last season. On a Rockford defense with few NHL-relevant prospects, there's opportunity for him.</p><p><b>Others on the radar:</b> Ashton Cumby, Paul Ludwinski, Julius Sumpf, Samu Alalauri</p>

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson is not here merely to win: 'We want to be feared'
entries.summary: <p>It’s just another morning at Halas Hall, nothing remarkable. It’s a couple hours until practice and about a month until <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ season starts, and it’s quiet. The sun shines softly on the dewy field near the building, and coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> can see it out the window of the X’s and O’s conference room.</p><p>Amid that tranquility, though, a fervor rises. It takes only a minute or so of talking competition and ambition to put him in motion. He rocks in his chair as he mentions that Super Bowl champions fade from people’s memories and how he wants more than that.</p><p>Not just wins, but domination. Not just scoring, but more points than any team in NFL history. Not just a Lombardi Trophy, but one that stands like a skyscraper the way <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/01/09/bears-qb-caleb-williams-1985-super-bowl-bears-rooting-for-him" >the 1985 Bears’ legacy still towers</a> four decades later. And not just one, but a dynasty.</p><p>He takes off his hat and runs his hand through his disheveled hair as he gets louder, and f-bombs burst into his sentences like popcorn. “Good, better, best” is his rallying cry in the locker room, but “Best ever or why bother?” is his true credo.</p><p>This is his baseline. This is his resting heartrate. He starts on 10.</p><p>“We want to be feared,” Johnson told the Sun-Times, every word edging closer toward the tone his players hear in practice. “We want shutouts on defense. We want blowouts on offense. That’s the mentality that we’re trying to embrace. It’s not, ‘Are we going to win?’ It’s, ‘How much are we going to win by?’ That’s what we live by.”</p><p>He's accelerating. This would be a terrible time to interrupt him.</p><p>“That’s how I grew up: We were dominant in youth league, we were dominant in middle school, we were dominant in high school, and that’s what I believe in,” he continued. “Hell, I still remember lining up and running ‘I Right 24 Sweep Dive’ 10 times in a row. Everyone knew what we were doing, and we were just, ‘Boom, boom, boom.’</p><p>“It was hardnosed, mountain football in North Carolina, and that is my backbone more so than any flashy offensive play there could ever be. It’s fundamentals, technique, effort. Those are the pillars of what we want to be about. It’s a differentiator at this level. Every team talks about it, but I don’t know that every team <i>is</i> about it.”</p><p>The Bears didn’t hire just an offensive mastermind last year. They got a psycho, in all the best ways. He gives his players a choice: Get on board and become as ruthless about this game as he is, or turn in your swipe card at the front desk on your way out.</p><p>That was a wakeup call to everyone, including quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>, in Johnson’s first training camp. Now it’s the Bears’ new normal.</p><p>Players come and go, and many of those who were on the field for the preseason opener against the Browns on Saturday won’t even be on the roster come September. Johnson was the most influential and important person the Bears had out there.</p><p>Everyone looks at Williams, for example, through the lens of how good Johnson can make him. The answer to questions about the reshuffled offensive line is that Johnson will figure it out. Even on defense, a major concern for the Bears this season, there’s trust that Johnson can solve any problem.</p><p>That belief ripples through Halas Hall and was reinforced by seven incredible comebacks last season, including a playoff win against the Packers. It propelled them to 11-6, an NFC North title and the divisional round of the postseason, where they lost in overtime to the Rams.</p><p>Veteran linebacker T.J. Edwards said Johnson fostered “a belief that we’ll make a play at the end of the game to win it,” and Williams echoed, “He’s provided that belief, that confidence.”</p><p>Emphatic endorsements rose from all corners of the locker room last season, and players weren’t talking like that about Matt Eberflus and Matt Nagy. Nagy was a fun coach at times, but never matched this intensity. Eberflus sounded lost at his introductory press conference and stayed that way.</p><p>Johnson couldn’t trace the exact spark of his fire, but knew with conviction it jumped to another level in 2018. He’d paid his dues as a Dolphins assistant coach for seven seasons to begin his career thinking it would lead to something, only to get coldly dismissed when they fired coach Adam Gase.</p><p>That made Johnson question everything, including the purpose of simply following along and waiting his turn.</p><p>“I didn’t know if I’d have another opportunity, so I said if I do, all hell’s breaking loose,” he said. “I’m going to just go full steam ahead and let the chips fall where they may. That’s been my mindset.</p><p>“I have zero fear of failure at this point. Hopefully the guys around me rally to that as well.”</p><p>That attitude made him a great fit with Lions coach Dan Campbell, who hired him to a low-level position and gradually promoted him to offensive coordinator. Holding fiercely to what he told himself in 2018, Johnson became the most innovative and overwhelming offensive coordinator in the league.</p><p>Packers safety Xavier McKinney complained in 2024 that the Lions’ offense set out to “embarrass people.” He was right. Johnson replied casually, “We’re trying to score a touchdown every time.”</p><p>There’s only one speed.</p><p>That’s why the playoff loss to the Rams still bothers Johnson even though the Bears went into last season widely predicted to be .500 at best. He couldn’t tolerate the idea of anything less than contending for a championship and was emboldened by a 9-3 start.</p><p>“When you get rolling like that and you have the confidence that you can win every single time you hit the grass, it hurts,” Johnson said. “I don’t care what the expectations were outside of the building to start the season. We had a lot of momentum going. So to fall short, it adds fuel to the fire for what we’re trying to accomplish this year.”</p><p>There’s a sense when sitting across from him that he could never be content. No matter what he achieves with the Bears, it won’t be enough. They’ve long needed someone that driven — a relentless, obsessive leader who brings that ferocity out of his players. There’s no doubt they have it now.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Former Spouse Accused of Murdering One of Her Offspring
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am writing for advice on how to be supportive of my adult children in light of an alleged crime committed by their mother. She was arrested for first-degree murder. The victim was my children's younger half-sibling.</p><p>I am especially challenged dealing with my daughter. She is supporting her mother in this. She says she has already lost a sibling and doesn't want to lose her mother too. Their mother was always critical of psychotherapy. Not only did she doubt it, but she criticized anyone seeking mental health support. Abby, now she's pleading not guilty by reason of insanity! How do I support and counsel my daughter? — <i>MANAGING THE REPERCUSSIONS</i></p><p><b>DEAR MANAGING:</b> Women in their right minds do not kill their children. Sometimes people are critical of mental health care because they're insecure about their own status. As upset as you are about this, your daughter has every right to support her mother through this tragedy if she wishes. The most effective way you can support your daughter would be to refrain from questioning her choice to be there for her mother.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> What are your thoughts about meeting another couple for lunch or dinner at a specific time only to find that they have already been seated and are enjoying appetizers? This has happened to us on numerous occasions, and, to us, it totally ruins the continuity of the meal together. We could understand it if we were late in arriving, but we're not. This has happened with more than one couple. — <i>FUMING IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR FUMING:</b> Personally, I think what they did is rude. However, it's one thing to be seated and chomp on a breadstick and quite another to be enjoying cocktails and calamari. It throws off the timing of the meal for the couple who arrive when they are supposed to. That said, when someone's blood sugar level drops, they may not be at their best, so it might be better to get some food than stand on ceremony.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a 48-year-old female who had to move in with my parents. It's not working. I know I am messy and tend to procrastinate. The issue is my mother. She constantly goes into my room to snoop. She tells me I'm worthless and dumb. Last night, I was eating a pork chop, and she said I was using the wrong knife. She took my knife and gave me a butter knife! I lost my job, so moving out isn't an option. But her comments and obvious disdain for me are not good for my self-esteem. Help! — <i>TRAPPED IN LONG BEACH</i></p><p><b>DEAR TRAPPED:</b> This advice may seem to come from left field, but I'm suggesting that you talk to your doctor about your messiness, procrastination and job situation. There may be a medical explanation for these issues. If there is, proper treatment may make a world of difference. However, if your problem isn't medical, your doctor can still refer you to a licensed family counselor who might help you coexist peacefully with your mom.</p><p>As for moving out, it's your best option in the long run. It's true that you're not ready now, but all your efforts must be focused on reaching that goal.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: Settlement reached in suit against Champaign doctor who left part of a fetus inside patient during abortion
entries.summary: <p>A lawsuit alleging a Champaign doctor performed a botched abortion was settled last month.</p><p>Dr. Keith Reisinger-Kindle was accused of leaving part of a fetus inside Michelle Hardy and puncturing a hole in her uterus while performing an abortion procedure at Champaign-based Equity Clinic in April 2023. When she started experiencing extreme cramping, Reisinger-Kindle allegedly told her to take Tylenol and laxatives.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/abortion/2025/03/23/champaign-abortion-doctor-lawsuit" target="_blank" >Hardy sued Reisinger-Kindle and Equity Clinic</a> in March 2025. They reached a settlement on July 8, according to court records.</p><p>Hardy's lawyer at the Chicago firm McNabola & Associates declined to comment. Reisinger-Kindle's lawyers at Pretzel & Stouffer did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Hardy, a mother of four, was about 22 weeks along when she sought an abortion from Reisinger-Kindle, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/abortion/2025/03/23/champaign-abortion-doctor-lawsuit" target="_blank" >according to her suit</a>. Two days after the procedure, she went to the emergency when she was still experiencing cramps.</p><p>That's when doctors found parts of the fetus in her right pelvis and surgically removed them. Doctors also found a hole in her uterus about the size of a quarter, according to the suit. Reisinger-Kindle allegedly refused to answer questions or share information with one of the surgeons who operated on Hardy.</p><p>In July 2025, Reisinger-Kindle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/07/08/champaign-doctor-abortion-keith-reisinger-kindle-health" target="_blank" >was disciplined by the state</a> and fined $5,000. He also had to complete 20 hours of continuing medical education for failing to properly evaluate a patient.</p>

entries.title: 2 women killed during separate arguments among the 4 people fatally shot overnight
entries.summary: <p>Four people were shot and killed overnight in Chicago, according to Chicago police.</p><p>A 35-year-old man was outside in the 4200 block of West Cermak Road in North Lawndale around midnight when an unknown person shot him in the chest and fled. The man was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, where he was pronounced dead. No one has been arrested, according to police.</p><p>An hour later in Englewood, two men were outside in the 1400 block of West 65th Street when someone inside a light-colored sedan fired several shots at them. One of the men, 30, was taken in critical condition to University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was later pronounced dead. The second man, 32, is in serious condition at Advocate Christ Medical Center. No one has been arrested, according to police.</p><p>A 38-year-old woman was in the 1300 block of West 13th Street in Little Italy with another person when they started arguing. The other person pulled out a gun about 3:40 a.m. and shot the woman in the chest then fled. The woman was taken to Stroger Hospital, where she was later pronounced dead. Police say no one has been arrested.</p><p>At around the same time in the Garfield Park neighborhood, another woman was arguing with an unknown man when he shot her several times in the body and her head in the 3800 block of West Harrison Street. He fled in a silver SUV. She was taken to Stroger, where she was pronounced dead. No one has been arrested, according to police.</p>

entries.title: Government keeps close tabs on delis, on funeral parlors not so much
entries.summary: <p>Burying a loved one is much harder than buying a corned beef sandwich. More expensive, too.</p><p>Trust me, I've done both.</p><p>When my mother died last year, my brother and I were immediately faced with a series of difficult decisions. She had bought burial plots in Colorado. Bury her there? I pictured the two of us standing in some windy nowhere in Boulder County, at a funeral attended by nobody else. No. We'd bury her here and put mountains on her grave marker — you can get those, for an additional charge.</p><p>Speaking of money. I floated an idea: donate the body to science? It would save, oh, $20,000 of our father's dwindling savings. That would pay for his care for, gee, almost three months.</p><p>"A funeral is part of doing the right thing," my brother said, invoking our mantra for handling our parents' affairs. So we had a funeral.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-360000" name="module-360000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>With a corned beef sandwich, there are also choices: Fatty or lean? Rye or a kaiser roll? Hot or cold? Don't forget condiments. But those are easier: fatty, rye, hot, yellow mustard. Far less expensive, too. At Kaufman's Bagel and Delicatessen in Skokie, it'll set you back $14.75.</p><p>Given the two experiences — the heart-rending, hugely-expensive funeral, and the pleasant, not-that-costly sandwich — why is it the state of Illinois so thoroughly inspects delis while so being so lax about monitoring funeral homes?</p><p>"I have so many inspections I can't see straight," said Bette Dworkin, owner of Kaufman's. "The Skokie Health Department, three times a year, a thorough inspection, inside and out. Weights and measures comes in. A whole list of backflow devices need to be tested."</p><p>Meanwhile, Illinois funeral directors are licensed but not the funeral homes the they operate, which are inspected when they open or change hands, and never inspected again, unless there is a complaint, and sometimes not even then. Which leads to periodic stomach-churning horrors, such as the 56 decomposing bodies found at a funeral home in South Deering, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" >documented in the Sun-Times</a> this past week.</p><p>Across the border is a much different situation.</p><p>"In the state of Wisconsin, there is licensing of the actual physical plant of the funeral home," said Michael D. Sharkey, a funeral director in Wisconsin for 30 years. "They do not do that in Illinois. When something goes wrong, nobody notices. That comes as a surprise to some people."</p><p>Sharkey is uniquely situated to compare the two states, being the legal representative of both the Wisconsin Funeral Directors Association and the Illinois Funeral Directors Association, as well as the associations in South Dakota and Minnesota, where he lives.</p><p>"The other big difference is that in Wisconsin, all regulatory actions are taken by the DSPS — the Department of Safety and Professional Services, all under one roof," he said. "In Illinois, the comptroller regulates crematories and the IDOFPR regulates funeral directors, two separate agencies."</p><p>Which leads to buck-passing.</p><p>"In Illinois, there is a lot of finger-pointing from agencies: It's not their job! It's somebody else's job!" said Sharkey. "Then you go to the next agency: 'That's not our job! That's somebody else's job!'"</p><p>Sharkey said Illinois authorities have 10 days to inspect a funeral home after a complaint.</p><p>"I think that's too long," he said, adding that in Minnesota, inspectors arrive within hours, police in tow, yellow tape at the ready to shut down a facility after a complaint.</p><p>What should happen in Illinois to stop horrors from happening?</p><p>Sharkey said state regulations are needed to put teeth in the inspection process.</p><p>"We're begging [Illinois]," he said. "Please do something."</p><p>In the meantime, how can consumers protect themselves when choosing funeral homes?</p><p>"Look to see if [a funeral home] is a member of the Illinois Funeral Directors Association." he said. "The IFDA has a very robust ethics committee and hold themselves to the highest standards. Those are the people you want to be dealing with."</p><p>A funeral is trying under the best of circumstances. The last thing you want to do is pay all that money and not get the service you deserve. Any fraud is awful to endure — a fraud perpetrated upon people at their moment of vulnerability and grief is especially cruel. Illinois can do better.</p><p>One of the decisions that had to be made was what, if anything, should go into my mother's coffin. My sister had sent her a box of candy, and I tucked it in, along with a stuffed elephant and her reading glasses. To do so, they opened the coffin. I took the opportunity to kiss her on the forehead and was glad I did, because she was cold. which helped me understand that she was really dead.</p>

entries.title: Northwestern says African Studies program isn’t closing. But staff told otherwise
entries.summary: <p>Northwestern University is changing the status of its Program of African Studies — described as the oldest African Studies program in the country — raising questions about how changes will impact everything from its funding to the staff.</p><p>University spokesperson Amy E. Lee said in a statement on Saturday <a class="Link" href="https://africanstudies.northwestern.edu/students/graduate/cluster.html" target="_blank" ><u>the program</u></a> “has not closed” but is “transitioning away from” its status as an Office for Research university-wide research institute and center."</p><p>“Northwestern values the important and impactful work of the Program of African Studies and remains committed to this work,” Lee said. "The university looks forward to engaging faculty to develop a shared direction for supporting African Studies at Northwestern.”</p><p>But Meagan Keefe, the program’s director of outreach and operations, told the Sun-Times in a phone interview that staff were informed Aug. 5 the program would close and they would no longer be employed as of Aug. 31.</p><p>Keefe said staff has not been provided specific details about where the program would be housed or what would happen to its funding. “They say it’s not closing, but they say we were let go because it closed. I don’t know how you have both,” she said.</p><h3>Program staffers uncertain about future</h3><p>Will Reno, a Northwestern political science department chair and professor who directed the program from 2012 to 2018, said two program staff members told him Aug. 5 they were being fired effective Aug. 31 .</p><p>"Normally, if you fire somebody, you’ve got to at least give them a heads-up. You’ve got certain rights," Reno said. "But if a program that they’re attached to is closing, you can tell these people, 'I’m sorry, the thing that you had a job at doesn’t exist.'"</p><p>Reno said to his knowledge faculty had not been notified of the decision beforehand.</p><p>“We don’t know the answer to the question of whether it’s closing,” Reno said.</p><p>He said faculty received a message from interim vice president for research Sumit Dhar on Aug. 7 explaining the program was not closing, though questions remained about what would happen after its two existing staff positions were eliminated. </p><h3>‘Damage’ done to NU’s reputation </h3><p>Reno said when he led the program, it had five staff members but slowly dwindled in recent years.</p><p>What initiated faculty interest was knowledge that the staffing of the Program of African Studies had suddenly been reduced to "zero," Reno said, leading to a perception that the program was shut down. </p><p>“We’re left adrift trying to figure out what zero [staff] means,” Reno said.</p><p>Reno said he heard from faculty, alumni groups and program donors worldwide since news of the change began circulating. </p><p>“I don’t think the administration understands the damage that this has caused,” he said. “They don’t understand the stakes.”</p><p>Reno explained he spent the weekend apologizing to program supporters and is concerned about the university's reputation over its decision. </p><p>"Our reputation as a university is dependent on people’s perceptions of our reputation," he said. "I’m getting all kinds of messages from people in the United States, but also people all around the world."</p><p>Founded in 1948, Northwestern’s <a class="Link" href="https://africanstudies.northwestern.edu/about/" target="_blank" ><u>Program of African Studies</u></a> has sponsored research on Africa and facilitated work within the continent, according to the program’s website.</p><p>Its interdisciplinary program has offered an undergraduate adjunct major and minor and a graduate certificate. It also provided administered grants and fellowships supporting research throughout the African diaspora.</p><p>“The university is committed to continued support for all facets of African Studies, including undergraduate and graduate education as well as research," Lee said. <br></p>

entries.title: Bulls coach Tiago Splitter not looking for part in arrested development
entries.summary: <p>It's a fair question to ask of Bulls coach Tiago Splitter, one that might not have a clear answer for a while. Maybe never.</p><p>Was breakout forward Deni Avdija already on a trajectory to go from draft disappointment with the Wizards to All-Star with the Trail Blazers last season or was it the coaching change of Chauncey Billups to Splitter just before the regular season that catapulted Avdija to become a foundation piece for an up-and-coming Western Conference team?</p><p>Tough to say.</p><p>The Bulls are hoping it’s the latter.</p><p>They have Matas Buzelis, a talented, versatile forward, and thoroughbred Caleb Wilson, 20, who has the skills to push for Rookie of the Year honors among a loaded 2026 draft class.</p><p>In other words, Splitter has a full plate.</p><p>As far as Avdija, he was taken No. 9 overall in the 2020 draft — Patrick Williams went No. 4 that year — and was more disappointment than promising prospect his first three seasons with the Wizards.</p><p>To his credit, however, Avdija started to show a jump in Year 4, bringing his average up from 9.2 points per game in 2022-23 to 14.7. He got to the free-throw line, improved his three-point shooting and, more important, started to show playmaking skills.</p><p>Of course, the Wizards gave up on him too early because that’s what they do, trading him to the Blazers on draft night in 2024 and giving the 2019-20 Israeli League MVP a new lease on life in the NBA.</p><p>Avdija showed signs in the 2024-25 season, but he really took off under Splitter. He averaged 24.2 points, and his assists went from 3.9 per game to 6.7. His free-throw numbers also climbed from 5.2 per game to 9.2.</p><p>Ball movement and attacking the rim with force are two aspects that Splitter stresses.</p><p>Coincidence?</p><p>The good news for Buzelis is, like Avdija, he’s coming off a season in which he averaged 16.3 points, and in the last 22 games of the regular season, he attacked the rim with aggression. His free throws went from 2.9 per game before the All-Star break to 3.6 the rest of the season.</p><p>The ingredients are there for Splitter to further unlock Buzelis.</p><p>And what about Wilson? Fans might have to pump the brakes a bit and realize he’s still a young player with a lot to learn, no matter how impressive he was in Summer League.</p><p>“[Everyone has] got to understand this is a process and not every night is going to be sunny and make all the shots,” Splitter said of Wilson and all the hype building around him. “It’s going to be up and down. But the trajectory has to be on an upward motion. That’s how we see it and part of the development.</p><p>“[Wilson has] got to also understand that part and that we’ve got a process going [for the] long run.”</p>

entries.title: 16 teens arrested at vacant Congress Theater, 1 week after illegal rave
entries.summary: <p>Sixteen teenagers were arrested at the Congress Theater Friday night nearly a week after police shut down an unsanctioned rave at the shuttered Logan Square venue. </p><p>Officers responded to a call for trespassing around 8:15 p.m. Friday in the 2100 block of North Milwaukee Avenue, Chicago police said. When the officers entered the theater, several people tried to flee.</p><p>The 16 teens, ages 13 to 19, were each charged with one misdemeanor count for criminal trespassing, according to police. Four were charged with reckless conduct, and two were cited for having pellet guns.</p><p>The mass arrest comes after a local DJ held an illegal rave at the theater Aug. 8 that drew several young people, according to Block Club Chicago. Police were called to shut it down, but officers did not arrest any of the attendees.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/14/landmark-congress-theater-federal-loan-preservation-finance-committee-city-council" target="_blank" >Plans are in the works to rehabilitate</a> the Congress Theater, which has sat vacant since 2013. With a $25.2-million federal loan and city grants, developers behind the renovation plan to once again make the theater an entertainment venue and add retail, office and residential spaces.</p><p>In his weekly newsletter, Ald. Daniel La Spata (1st) condemned the rave and said it slowed down the rehab effort. </p><p>"Participants did significant damage to the building, substantially increasing the cost of its rehabilitation," La Spata wrote. The rave also "required police response that distracted from much more important matters."</p><p>La Spata did not immediately reply to a request for comment Sunday. </p>

entries.title: Former first-round pick Marcus Davenport visits DE-needy Bears
entries.summary: <p>Free agent defensive end Marcus Davenport, a former first-round draft pick, visited the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>. For a team that added no relevant pass rushers this offseason, Davenport represents a big name. Still, he has just four sacks in the past four seasons after posting nine in 2021. </p><p>Davenport knows the Bears, and vice versa — he played for defensive coordinator Dennis Allen with the Saints from 2018-22. After a year with the Vikings, he played two seasons with the Lions. Bears head coach <a class="Link" href="http://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/16/bears-coach-ben-johnson-is-not-here-merely-to-win-we-want-to-be-feared" target="_blank" >Ben Johnson</a> worked on the Lions staff in 2024. He started seven games for the Lions last year but wasn't particularly effective — Pro Football Focus ranked him 103rd out of 115 qualified edge rushers.</p><p>The Saints drafted him 14th overall in 2018.</p><p>The Bears got some good news at defensive end — Montez Sweat returned to practice Sunday for the first time since he left Aug. 6. Johnson said Saturday he expected him back soon.</p>

entries.title: Bears LT Ozzy Trapilo returns from Physically Unable to Perform list
entries.summary: <p>Ozzy Trapilo is back.</p><p>The left tackle whom the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> feared would miss most, if not all of the 2026 season with a torn patellar tendon, was activated off the Physically Unable to Perform list shortly before Sunday's practice. </p><p>When it became clear to the Bears that Trapilo's rehab was ahead of schedule, they decided they wanted to see him practice in full — and in pads — during training camp. Sunday marked the first step toward that goal.</p><p>Week 1 is four weeks away. Trapilo's return to game action, whenever that may happen, will a boon to the team's left tackle search. Braxton Jones was leading a three-person race before hurting his knee earlier this month. He returned to practice Wednesday in a limited capacity. </p><p>Trapilo started six times at left tackle last year and seemed to be the team's answer at the position for 2026 before suffering the serious knee injury in the playoff win against the Packers.</p><p>"There's others that never come back from it ... " offensive line coach Dan Roushar said Thursday. "I've said this to him a number of times — I'd rather be a day too late than a day too early putting him on the field. As he integrates back to practice, he's gonna have to demonstrate that he can — and we have to make sure that we're not pushing him beyond his comfort level, his boundaries of his health. ... It'll be a process. His actions in practice will demonstrate to us his readiness."</p><p>Kiran Amegadjie and Jedrick Wills split snaps in Saturday's exhibition game <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/08/15/bears-browns-podcast-tyson-bagent-ben-johnson" target="_blank" >against the Browns</a>. Offensive coordinator Press Taylor said both were inconsistent.</p><p>"It wasn't as clean as we'd love it to be going forward," he said. "And that's kind of why there still continues to be an open competition for the position. But I think there were some encouraging things we continue to teach from and coach from and grow from."</p><p>The Bears waived three players with injury designations: cornerback KC Eziomume, receiver Kyron Hudson and safety Gervarrius Owens.</p>

entries.title: Cubs shortstop Dansby Swanson leaves game with apparent injury
entries.summary: <p>One of the Cubs’ most durable players might have gotten injured.</p><p>Shortstop Dansby Swanson left Sunday’s game against the Cardinals in the bottom of the third inning after swinging through a 0-0 Hunter Dobbins pitch. Swanson immediately grimaced in pain and was replaced by pinch-hitter James Triantos.</p><p>Swanson has played in 119 of the Cubs’ 125 games.</p><p>The Cubs trailed St. Louis 3-0 when Swanson departed.</p><p>In the top of the fourth, Nico Hoerner shifted to shortstop and Triantos stayed in at second base.</p><p>The team said Swanson had left side discomfort.</p>

entries.title: Brenton Doyle, Tristan Peters getting along just fine in White Sox' outfield
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — The White Sox’ trade for center fielder Brenton Doyle on Aug. 3 had the potential to create tension in the team’s utopian clubhouse.</p><p>Incumbent center fielder Tristan Peters had a first half that put him in the All-Star Game, but he was having a rough start to the second half. Doyle had missed more than two months with an oblique injury, but his resume included two Gold Gloves with the Rockies.</p><p>Though the plan was to platoon them — Peters gets righties, Doyle lefties — Peters couldn’t be blamed for looking over his shoulder, wondering if the new guy might steal some playing time.</p><p>But that hasn’t been the case.</p><p>“It’s exciting seeing somebody come in,” Peters told the Sun-Times. “We’ve had a few because of the deadline. It’s exciting meeting new guys and seeing what they can do and how they can benefit the team, as well. Brenton is an incredible outfielder. It’s been fun playing the outfield with him, too.”</p><p>That last part has been interesting to see. Manager Will Venable has played Peters in left some with Doyle in center. Considering that center fielders’ job is to take charge in the outfield, they’ve worked on communicating when Peters plays left. That came in handy when Peters ran toward the gap and made a leaping catch at the wall against the Reds last week at Rate Field.</p><p>“There’s definitely times on balls in the gaps like that where you have two very athletic, fast outfielders that both could get to the ball,” Doyle told the Sun-Times. “Communication is very important. That’s something we work on when we practice. That play he had against the wall was a really good catch.”</p><p>Through that communication, Doyle and Peters have become chummy quickly.</p><p>“Tristan’s one of the guys that I’ve gotten closest to so far here,” Doyle said. “Tristan’s a very good center fielder. I don’t think there’s any bad blood being created with me playing center field. I haven’t gotten any hints of anything like that. Tristan’s a great guy. We just understand our roles.”</p><p>Doyle said he has felt welcomed since arriving and is enjoying the easygoing atmosphere in the clubhouse.</p><p>“A lot of good energy, a lot of good vibes,” he said. “They just make it easy to fit right in.”</p><h3>Braden has strong series</h3><p>Rookie Braden Montgomery had an impressive series against the Tigers, going 3-for-5 with three RBI on Friday, driving in a run with two outs Saturday and going 1-for-4 with a walk Sunday. Hitting coach Derek Shomon credited Montgomery for working through some rough stretches, as well as cutting back on his pregame work.</p><p>“Trim some fat on the routine side of things and limit the opportunity to get frustrated early in the day by overworking yourself,” Shomon said Sunday. “He’s done a really nice job of condensing it and grabbing what he needs pregame to feel like he’s most prepared. So he’s done an awesome job, and he’s certainly getting more acclimated at this level.”</p><p>Venable certainly agrees. Since the All-Star break, Montgomery has played every inning of every game except for his day off Aug. 2.</p><h3>Sam turns to torpedo bat</h3><p>Shomon said left-handed hitter Sam Antonacci has been using a torpedo bat against lefties to “put him in a better spot to get barrell to the baseball.”</p><p>Antonacci has been hitting better against lefties since the All-Star break, raising his batting average to .237. And Venable has been playing him more against lefties. In the Reds series last week, Antonacci started in both games against left-handers, batting eighth. He generally leads off against right-handers.</p><p>The impact that both Antonacci and Montgomery have had as rookies is notable.</p><p>“It speaks largely to the development chain,” Shomon said. “You look through the minor leagues and the things that are going on there with our player-development group, so kudos to them. entries.title: Former manager David Ross feels no awkwardness in Cubs locker room
entries.summary: <p>If you saw him before Sunday’s game and didn’t know better, you’d think <b>David Ross </b>was just another journalist working at Wrigley Field. Wearing a pale blue shirt, a credential around his neck and carrying a notebook, Ross chatted with players on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> and Cardinals and didn’t look much different from the people in the press box, albeit a little taller and more physically imposing than the stereotypical scribe.</p><p>But unlike the reporters, Ross once drew thunderous cheers as the beloved veteran on the 2016 champions. His success and reputation as a player set him up to manage the Cubs, which he did for four seasons.</p><p>And then unceremoniously, Ross’ tenure in the Cubs dugout ended. He was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2023/11/6/23949204/cubs-will-hire-craig-counsell-to-replace-david-ross-as-manager" >fired in Nov. 2023</a> so the Cubs could hire <b>Craig Counsell</b>. Ross hasn’t managed since, and as part of his duties as an analyst for Sunday’s ABC broadcast, he walked in the same areas where he was the boss and a celebrity player not too long ago.</p><p>This time, however, he was a visitor calling a game at Wrigley for the first time after the dismissal.</p><p>“I like walking into the locker room and seeing the guys that played for me, like <b>Nico </b>[<b>Hoerner</b>],” Ross told the Sun-Times inside the St. Louis locker room. “I don’t feel any awkwardness. I had a lot of good memories in that locker room. It’s a great spot.”</p><h2><b>Moving things around</b></h2><p>To make room for <b>Edward Cabrera</b>, the Cubs optioned <b>Javier Assad </b>to Triple-A Iowa. Moving Assad and his 2.35 ERA since May 5 to Iowa wasn’t a reflection of his performance.</p><p>“The decision we made was just to preserve every pitcher we could,” Counsell said. “Certainly, from Javy’s shoes, that doesn’t feel fair, but from a depth perspective this was a way to preserve everybody and keep maximum depth and move forward.”</p><p>Assad’s next appearance will be as a starter for Iowa.</p><p>Meanwhile, <b>David Peterson </b>is heading to the Cubs’ bullpen. And like Assad, the decision with Peterson probably wasn’t based on stats. Over his last six starts, Peterson had a 2.14 ERA over 33 2/3 innings, but was squeezed out of the rotation by the arrivals of <b>Kevin Gausman </b>and <b>Clay Holmes</b>.</p><h2><b>First things first</b></h2><p><b>Pedro Ramirez </b>started at first base to give <b>Michael Busch </b>a day off. Busch has started 122 of the Cubs’ 125 games, while Sunday was Ramirez’s inaugural start at first.</p><p>Though the Cubs were glad to give Busch a breather, there was more to the decision.</p><p>If Busch goes down, the Cubs don’t have much experience at first base. Other than Ramirez, <b>Carson Kelly</b>, <b>James Triantos </b>and <b>Matt Shaw </b>would also be candidates to step in, but none of those options are perfect. Kelly’s only played at first four times, Shaw is still on the injured list and Triantos has never played the position professionally.</p><p>“We need to get somebody that’s, at a certain point of the season, is comfortable playing there should a need arise,” Counsell said. “We need to get someone at first base.”</p><p>Counsell said he “fully anticipates” Shaw being back from the sprained left hand that’s sidelined him since June 28.</p>

entries.title: No. 3 Loyola shakes off last season, looks ahead with a talented core and the return of John Holecek
entries.summary: <p>The preseason talk at Loyola is all about returning to “the standard.” The Ramblers finished 4-5 last year, a shocking record taken at face value. But it is important to remember that Loyola’s young team gave Mount Carmel a stern test in the first round of the Class 8A playoffs.</p><p>John Holecek, the Ramblers’ head coach from 2006 through 2022, is back at the helm after spending one year away from the program and the last two as an assistant coach.</p><p>“[Holecek] is back and the standard is a little different now,” senior linebacker Will Mettee, a Boston College recruit, said. “We need to make sure everyone is on the same page all the time. Last year that wasn’t always the case. We always had these little misses on defense and offense.”</p><p>Mettee (6-1, 225 pounds) leads a strong linebacker core rounded out by two juniors, Mark Atwood and Barrett Schifferdecker.</p><p>“They are excellent, tough, athletic kids,” Holecek said. “On the defensive line [Braedan McHugh and Winston Ericson] aren’t Power Four-looking kids but are explosive and tough. They are stout with great technique and quickness.”</p><p>Loyola is No. 3 in the preseason Super 25 and picked up two talented transfers who will contribute on defense: lineman Hunter Wahtola, a North Dakota recruit, and defensive back Patrick Carnel.</p><p>The Ramblers played two quarterbacks throughout last season: Dom Maloney and Matthew Lee, a highly regarded college prospect. Lee will start this season, but Holecek says Maloney will play some quarterback. The senior is also starting at safety.</p><p>“It’s been a lot of work learning the new offense and also safety,” Maloney said. “Super hard but super fun. Anything I can do to help the team. We have to use last year as fuel. Everyone is expecting us to be like the team was last year, but we have expectations to go back to state and win.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: White Sox outfielders better be ready for the heckling confines of Wrigley Field
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> didn’t hear much vitriol from the home crowd during their sweep of the Tigers, which they capped with a 7-5 victory Sunday. Despite putting a dent in the Tigers’ playoff hopes, the first-place Sox didn’t quite draw the fans’ ire.</p><p>They don’t need to be in first to get Cubs fans’ dander up, though. The Sox would get an earful at Wrigley Field just for being there, but they’re especially at risk this week after Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong took a tongue-lashing at Rate Field in May.</p><p>“I think we know what the crowd’s going to be like,” manager Will Venable said after his team took a season-high 5½-game lead in the American League Central. “It’s going to be a great atmosphere.”</p><p>That might depend on your point of view. Sox outfielders figure to bear the brunt of the abuse after a woman sitting in the Rate Field picnic area May 17 yelled “You suck!” at Crow-Armstrong, whose profane response earned him a $5,000 fine from MLB.</p><p>If fans follow baseball’s old unwritten rules, whereby a pitcher retaliates for a hit batter by plunking that player’s counterpart, Brenton Doyle and Tristan Peters better pack earplugs in their pockets.</p><p>Peters, for one, has no idea what’s coming. The series opener Monday will be his first game at the not-always Friendly Confines.</p><p>“I really don’t know what to expect,” he said. “But I’m excited.”</p><p>Doyle has a better idea. He has played on the North Side eight times with the Rockies. In his last game there in May 2025, Doyle hit a tying home run in the seventh inning off Cade Horton that traveled 371 feet, landing in the front row of the left-field bleachers.</p><p>“The fans definitely get loud out there,” he said. “It’s a cool experience, the ivy and everything. The energy is also super great. They have some passionate fans there, and they let you know about it.”</p><p>Has he ever talked with any bleacher bums?</p><p>“No. No conversations,” he said.</p><p>That’s probably for the best.</p><p>Had Crow-Armstrong kept his mouth shut, he could’ve saved himself some cash.</p><p>First baseman Munetaka Murakami, whose two-run homer in the seventh Sunday put the Sox ahead to stay, has a good idea of what awaits in his first visit to Wrigley.</p><p>“It’ll be crazy,” he said through an interpreter. “The last series at Rate Field was obviously a great series with big crowds. It’s going to be a dogfight, but we’re gonna be confident.”</p><p>Starter Sean Burke, who battled through 4⅓ innings to keep the Sox in the game, has pitched at Wrigley once, allowing five earned runs in 4 ⅔ innings of a Sox loss in May 2025.</p><p>“It’s going to be fun,” he said. “Honestly, I’m a little bummed I’m not pitching in it. It’s going to be cool to watch as a bystander and take in the environment.”</p><p>Truth be told, there will be plenty of Sox fans in attendance, certainly in the bleachers. So Crow-Armstrong might not exactly be spared from more heckling.</p><p>The best thing the Sox can do is take care of business the way they did against the Tigers, whose successful run despite trading top pitchers Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize was short-lived. Though Venable doesn’t see the Sox’ sweep as a statement, it most definitely is.</p><p>“Call it whatever you want,” he said. “I’m just so proud of the group.”</p><p>He also doesn’t see his team as “surprising,” though it most definitely is.</p><p>“Really from spring training, these guys believed, and they continue to believe,” he said. “We know what’s ahead of us here. But we’re not into making statements.”</p><p>Cubs fans will have plenty of those ready to go, and the Sox’ best response would be a finger pressed to their lips.</p><p>Not that finger!</p><div entries.title: Yankees icon Derek Jeter tells Bears not to focus on failure
entries.summary: <p>Derek Jeter never thought about failing.</p><p>When the Yankees legend was preparing for a big moment, he’d think back to all the moments he had success — even if it was on the basketball court at Kalamazoo (Mich.) Central High School.</p><p>That was the message that the Baseball Hall of Famer and 14-time All-Star shortstop gave <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> players and coaches a team meeting last week — to forget about failure.</p><p>“He’s known as being one of the most clutch players of our generation,” offensive coordinator Press Taylor said before Sunday’s practice. “He talked about, ‘When I had an opportunity for it, I went back to the last time I had success. I didn’t think about the time I failed in this moment.’</p><p>“He talked about going back to, he was a sophomore in high school and scoring the game-winning basket. That’s what he’s thinking about when he’s in Game 7 of the World Series up to bat in a critical moment. He’s thinking of ‘the time I succeeded.’”</p><p>Linebacker Jon Rhattigan, who called the Yankees great an “icon,” said that he focused on “universal truths” that apply to both baseball and football: trusting your teammates, focusing and working hard.</p><p>“I think his approach to the game of baseball can help our approach individually to the game of football,” he said.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/16/bears-training-camp-former-first-round-pick-marcus-davenport-visits-defensive-end-needy" target="_blank" >Bears</a> produced a clip of Jeter that listed his accomplishments and aired it before bringing him to the front of the Halas Hall meeting room. Jeter played from 1999-2014, retiring when the youngest Bears player was just 10.</p><p>“Great lessons,” said guard Joe Thuney, who is 33. “A guy who's so successful, and such a great leader — it's awesome when people can come in like that and give you their opinions and thoughts. I learned a lot from him.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox at Cubs — the Crosstown Come-Up — takes the stage Monday, a series this city deserves
entries.summary: <p>Wrigley Field is way better than Rate Field.</p><p><i>Way better at attracting frat bros, you mean?</i></p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> are the best team in the city.</p><p><i>The </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><i>White Sox</i></a><i> are more fun.</i></p><p>Our record is better.</p><p><i>So? We’re in first place.</i></p><p>Blue.</p><p><i>Black.</i></p><p>Wiener’s Circle.</p><p><i>Ricobene’s.</i></p><p>North Side!</p><p><i>South Side!</i></p><p>Why am I arguing with myself?</p><p><i>I was about to ask you the same thing.</i></p><p>*****************</p><p>Look, sorry if that was a strange way to start a column. It’s just that the Cubs and Sox are squaring off against each other again starting on Monday, and both teams are actually — what’s that word? — winning. That’s such a rarity, it’ll be only the second time in 18 years both teams bring winning records into Wrigley. And it’ll be the first time not counting the 2020 pandemic season, when the stands were so utterly empty, no one was around to beat the hell out of one another in hopes of going viral. Talk about sad.</p><p>Anyway, this — the Crosstown Come-Up, I’m calling it — feels like such a big deal for a change that it seemed appropriate to warm up with a little smack talk.</p><p>Speaking of smack talk …</p><p>“Kudos to the White Sox for consistently putting themselves in position to be where they are now — first place — which is very impressive,” Cubs shortstop Dansby Swanson said before taking the field Sunday against the Cardinals.</p><p>OK, so it wasn’t exactly in the spirit of a Michael Barrett punch to the face of A.J. Pierzynski. But maybe we’ll get back to that level of Cubs-Sox craziness eventually.</p><p>Swanson probably should have told me to buzz off when I asked him about the Sox, specifically about the teams’ series at Rate Field back in mid-May. The Cubs entered that series in first place, 2½ games up on the Brewers and Cardinals, but dropped the last two to the Sox to begin what turned into a hard-to-believe 10-game losing streak, by the end of which the Cubs were 4½ games behind the Brewers and in last place. Three months later, I wanted to know, are the Cubs too strong a team to take another disastrous turn?</p><p>“Anything can happen, but this group knows what it’s capable of and believes in itself,” Swanson said. “We have a lot of good momentum and energy.”</p><p>Then Swanson took the field and — disaster alert — had to leave the game right in the middle of his first at-bat. Swanson, who prides himself more than most on playing every day, swung through a Hunter Dobbins fastball in the third inning and was grimacing before the barrel finished traveling through the zone. He dropped the bat, threw down his helmet, walked straight to the dugout and, gosh, how bad might this be?</p><p>You want to blame me, go ahead.</p><p>“I didn’t even think this group would go through a stretch like that,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said about the losing streak.</p><p>No one did. That’s because it was preceded by a pair of Cubs 10-game winning streaks. Three months ago, the Cubs strutted down to the South Side at a time when baseball writers all over were putting them at or near the very top of major league power rankings.</p><p>That felt pretty off base by the time the Sox’ Edgar Quero — who’s in Triple-A now — belted an extra-inning walk-off homer to win the rubber game against the Cubs in one of the most exciting Crosstown games in memory. Then the Cubs kept losing, even getting swept by the Brewers in three games at Wrigley. For at least a minute there, the Sox were legitimately the city’s better club.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Edgar Quero’s first home run of the season is a walk-off HR.<br><br>Quero is the first Chicago White Sox catcher to hit a walk-off home run against the Chicago Cubs. <a href="https://t.co/gM8mlc7VNW">pic.twitter.com/gM8mlc7VNW</a></p>— Francys Romero (@FrancysRomero) <a href="https://x.com/FrancysRomero/status/2056126004318314580?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 17, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“It’s exciting. I think it’s great for baseball and great for the city,” Hoerner said. “We’ve always had great atmospheres playing the White Sox, regardless of if we’re having a good year, they’re having a good year or either of us is struggling. But this feels even more so. It’s later in the season and both teams have playoff hopes, and it just makes for a great series.”</p><p>Before the first series, the Cubs actually were cooling off, having dropped two of three in Texas and then in Atlanta heading in. This time, they go in having been torched by the Cardinals over the weekend in back-to-back 8-4 and 11-4 defeats.</p><p>The Sox, meanwhile, have both feet on the gas pedal after sweeping the Tigers in Detroit. The Sox homered nine times against the Cubs, with Munitaka Murikami, Miguel Vargas and Colson Montgomery each going yard multiple times. Murikami and Vargas come in red hot for the rematch, having bombed away a combined five times in three games while writing the Tigers’ season obituary.</p><p>Who would’ve believed coming into the season that one of Chicago’s teams would have a 5½-game division lead with six weeks to go, and that would be the gang from 13 Red Line stops south of Wrigley?</p><p>Swanson has never been on a Red Line train, but Hoerner has.</p><p>How about a Red Line World Series this year? Or, you know, ever?</p><p>“That would be absolutely all-time,” Hoerner said. “And I’d be all for it.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/16/cubs-shortstop-dansby-swanson-leaves-game-with-apparent-injury" >Cubs shortstop Dansby Swanson heading to injured list</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears RB Kyle Monangai leaves practice after hurting right knee
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> running back Kyle Monangai left practice Sunday after appearing to hurt his right knee.</p><p>Monangai got tangled with defensive tackle Grady Jarrett during a drill. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/15/bears-browns-final-score-34-10-quarterback-tyson-bagent-didnt-meet-own-standard-ben-johnson-trade-shepherd-nfl" target="_blank" >Bears</a> players were not wearing full pads. Initial indications were promising that he avoided serious injury, a source said, though the team still needed further testing to be sure.</p><p>About half the Bears' roster participated in Sunday's practice, which began roughly 24 hours after the conclusion of Saturday's exhibition win against the Browns. Monangai did not play in that game, nor did most of the Bears' relevant offensive players.</p><p>A seventh-round pick from Rutgers, Monangai had an eye-opening rookie year, running 169 times for 783 yards last season. He started one game, during which he ran for 176 yards in a win against the Bengals.</p><p>He entered training camp entrenched behind starter D'Andre Swift. Behind him are question marks: Roschon Johnson, Salvon Ahmed, Coleman Bennett and Brittain Brown. Johnson led the Bears in carries and rushing yards Saturday. Ahmed scored a 49-yard touchdown on a screen pass.</p><p>Swift and Monangai were shockingly durable last year, handling all but eight carries given to Bears running backs.</p><p>Bears players were concerned about Monangai when he went down — chief among them Jarrett. Monangai was examined by a trainer and walked to the locker room.</p><p>“Hopefully it’s nothing too crazy significant,” guard Joe Thuney said. “But football is football. It’s tough.”<br></p>

entries.title: Tommy John, namesake for a pioneering elbow surgery that saved his career, dead at 83
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES — Tommy John, who won 288 games during a 26-year big league career and became the first pitcher to successfully return following groundbreaking elbow surgery that later was named after him, has died. He was 83.</p><p>He died at his home in Bradenton, Florida, on Saturday night, agent Mike Maguire said Sunday. He had been in hospice care.</p><p>On Aug. 8, the New York Yankees released a social media post in which John wrote that he wanted to say goodbye to everyone, including friends and fans who followed him throughout his career, saying, “I will never forget you.”</p><p>The Yankees called John “a bedrock of our rotation during his time in pinstripes and a longtime favorite of Yankees fans.”</p><p>John was a four-time All-Star with a record of 288-231 and a 3.34 ERA during a career that stretched from 1963 to 1989. He pitched for Cleveland, the Chicago White Sox, the Los Angeles Dodgers, the Yankees, the California Angels and the Oakland Athletics.</p><p>“Tommy was an exceptional pitcher throughout his career in Major League Baseball, and his courageous role in becoming the first to have surgery that would go on to bear his name can’t be overstated,” Stan Kasten, Dodgers president and CEO, said in a statement. "His impact both on and off the field has been felt by ballplayers of all ages and will be for generations to come.”</p><p>The left-hander was 31 years old when he tore the ulnar collateral ligament in his pitching elbow in 1974, a death knell for pitchers' careers to that point.</p><p>John allowed Dr. Frank Jobe, the Dodgers’ team physician, to replace the ligament with a tendon from his right forearm. Jobe gave the surgery 100-to-1 odds of being successful.</p><p><b>John was a great pitcher, but his elbow surgery made him a baseball legend</b></p><p>The procedure had been done on others before, although it was usually performed on wrists and hands. John was the first pitcher to have it done on his elbow.</p><p>More than 2,600 big leaguers and thousands more amateurs have since had UCL reconstructions, better known as Tommy John surgery. It’s been a godsend for many of baseball’s greatest stars, including two-way sensation Shohei Ohtani, three-time Cy Young Award winner Justin Verlander and even Philadelphia Phillies slugger Bryce Harper.</p><p>“If you put it in dollars and cents, I think there’s no question that Tommy John is the most valuable reconstructive procedure there is,” Dodgers team physician Dr. Neal ElAttrache told The Associated Press in 2024.</p><p>Born Thomas Edward John Jr. on May 22, 1943, in Terre Haute, Indiana, he was a top baseball and basketball player at the city’s Gerstmeyer High. He graduated in 1961 as valedictorian but did not give the commencement speech because of a stutter. Despite being recruited by the University of Kentucky to play basketball, John chose baseball and signed with Cleveland.</p><p>“The day I left for my first job as a pitcher, my father looked at me & said, ‘Good luck, Tommy. Just remember one thing: whether you make it big in the big leagues or you don’t, you’ll always just be Tommy John from Terre Haute, Indiana.’ I’ve never forgotten those words,” John wrote in his Aug. 8 post.</p><p>John recorded 2,245 strikeouts but never led either league in wins or strikeouts. He had the second-most wins of any pitcher since 1900 not to be elected to the Hall of Fame. From 1995 through 2009, John was on the Hall of Fame ballot, but he never received more than 31.7% of the votes, falling well short of the 75% required for election.</p><p>“Tommy was a wonderful person who competed to the utmost and did what no player had ever done to save his career, in conjunction with the esteemed Dr. Frank Jobe,” former Dodgers general manager Ned Colletti posted on X. “The HOF is missing Tommy John.”</p><p><b>John won more games after his eponymous surgery</b></p><p>Known for his longevity, John was the opening day starter for both the 1966 Chicago White Sox and the 1989 New York Yankees. He won 124 games before his UCL repair and 164 after. His final appearance came days after his 46th birthday.</p><p>“While his incredible longevity and post-surgery achievements changed the fortunes and trajectory of countless athletes around the world, it also overshadowed his excellence as a pitcher,” the Yankees said in a statement. “We pause to remember the totality of his legacy — his competitiveness and skill, his penchant for conversation, his kind and gracious nature, and his stature as an athletic and medical pioneer.”</p><p>John made his major league debut on Sept. 6, 1963, pitching one inning in relief for Cleveland.</p><p>He was traded to the White Sox in 1965 and worked his way into the starting rotation. The following year, he tied for the American League lead with five shutouts and in 1967, his six shutouts led the AL.</p><p>In 1971, he was traded to the Dodgers.</p><p>In 1974, John had a 13-3 record and led the National League in victories going into the All-Star break. He was pitching against the Montreal Expos when he permanently damaged the UCL in his left arm. After a month, the injury had not improved.</p><p>During the four-hour surgery on Sept. 25, 1974, Jobe made holes in the humerus and ulna bones of John’s left arm and used anchors to insert the tendon in a figure-eight pattern.</p><p>At first, John’s left hand was shriveled and he lacked feeling in several of his fingers because of damage to the ulnar nerve. Jobe performed a second procedure to reroute the nerve that was necessary to John’s full recovery.</p><p>John’s arm was in a cast for four months. He had recovered the full range of motion in his left arm by spring training of 1975 and spent that season resting, healing and rebuilding strength in his arm. John worked with fellow Dodgers pitcher Mike Marshall, who had a doctorate in kinesiology, on learning a different grip.</p><p>That September he made five appearances during an offseason instructional league, working his way up to seven innings by his final game.</p><p>John resumed pitching for the Dodgers in 1976 as the fourth starter in their rotation. He allowed three runs in five innings and took the loss in his first start against Atlanta, the first time any pitcher had started a game following UCL reconstructive surgery.</p><p>John donated the original cast from his surgery to the Smithsonian Institution in June 2022. His teammates on the 1974 Dodgers signed it, as well as Jobe and the team’s Hall of Fame announcer Vin Scully.</p><p>The procedure has become so widely known that in 2019, Merriam-Webster added the term to its dictionary.</p><p>John made 31 starts for the Dodgers in 1976, posting a 10-10 record, a 3.09 ERA, 91 strikeouts, 61 walks and 207 hits allowed in 207 innings.</p><p>In 1977, he won 20 games for the first time in his career, finishing with a 20-7 record. He finished second behind Philadelphia’s Steve Carlton in voting for the NL Cy Young Award.</p><p><b>John and his family had mixed feelings about the legacy of his operation</b></p><p>Over 50 years later, Tommy John surgery is as much a part of baseball as peanuts and hot dogs. Advanced training methods are helping pitchers of all ages throw harder than ever. They take comfort knowing a torn UCL won’t necessarily end their careers.</p><p>“I am sick my name is attached to a surgery happening in kids more than pros,” John tweeted in July 2018.</p><p>John’s oldest son, Tommy III, became a chiropractor who wrote a book suggesting ways to prevent young athletes from having to undergo major sports-related surgery similar to what his father endured.</p><p>After his pitching career ended, John worked as a broadcaster for the Minnesota Twins and Yankees in the 1990s. He managed the Bridgeport (Connecticut) Bluefish from 2007-09.</p><p>John was hospitalized in December 2020 because of COVID-19 and later had Guillain-Barré syndrome, in which a person’s immune system attacks their nerves. John told the New York Post in May 2022 that he was paralyzed in his lower extremities for several months.</p><p>John and his wife Sally Simmons had four children: Tamara, Tommy III, Travis and Taylor, who died of a prescription drug overdose at 28 in 2010. The couple divorced in 2013.</p><p>Besides his children, he is survived by his second wife, Cheryl, and son-in-law Patrick Mannelly, a retired NFL long snapper who played 16 years for the Chicago Bears.<br></p>
